logline: A prosecutor with a surgically severed emotional response and a police lieutenant form an unlikely alliance to expose corruption winding from a murder case deep into the South Korean legal establishment.

renewal.note: Two-season run concluded with Season 2 on October 4, 2020. No further seasons announced; creator Lee Soo-yeon has not signalled a return.

bollymeter.basis: Season 1 was named one of the New York Times' Best TV Shows of 2017 and won the Grand Prize at the 54th Baeksang Arts Awards. Critics consistently praised its tightly plotted corruption thriller and lead performances.

pull_quotes.text: The plot was constantly moving forward, the suspense was nicely kept until the end.

seasons.review_body: Season 1 of Stranger arrived on tvN in June 2017 and quickly earned a reputation as one of the sharpest crime thrillers in Korean television history. The New York Times ranked it tenth among the Best TV Shows of 2017, and it swept the 54th Baeksang Arts Awards, with Cho Seung-woo taking Best Actor and Lee Soo-yeon winning Best Screenplay. Critics clustered around two virtues: the cold-logic procedural rigour anchored by a prosecutor clinically incapable of feeling, and the institutional corruption anatomy that felt bracingly real. Bae Doona's police lieutenant brings warmth that offsets the show's icy intelligence. With 16 episodes and zero filler, the season operates as a near-perfect closed argument about what happens when institutions betray the people inside them.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 1
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The cold open establishes the show's signature register: a murder, a prosecutor who cannot feel fear, and a legal system whose every corridor smells of rot. Confident world-building from minute one.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Hwang Shi-mok calmly processing a crime scene while colleagues show visible distress signals the entire show's thesis in a single image.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 16
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The finale pays off the season's intricate setup without resorting to a triumphant resolution - justice here is partial, incremental, and hard-won, which is precisely the point.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The final exchange between Shi-mok and Yeo-jin lands not as a celebration but as a quiet acknowledgment that the fight simply continues.

bollymeter.basis: Critic Jae-Ha Kim awarded 3/4 stars, noting it 'didn't hold as much dramatic tension as the first season' but the lead performances made it must-see viewing. Audience consensus tracks similarly.

pull_quotes.text: While it didn't hold as much dramatic tension as the first season, the one-two punch of the series stars made it must-see viewing.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 aired in the summer of 2020 and shifted focus from a single murder to a jurisdictional power struggle between the Prosecution and the Police as institutional reform legislation loomed. The political architecture is more complex but the emotional stakes are lower - critics noted the absence of the first season's visceral tension, even as they praised Cho Seung-woo and Bae Doona's partnership. Jae-Ha Kim, covering Korean drama for international outlets, awarded 3/4 stars and observed that the season demonstrated a K-drama can hold viewer interest without romance or a second-lead rivalry. The open ending left room for a third season, though none has materialised as of mid-2026.
seasons.season_over_season: Broader political canvas than Season 1 but quieter personal stakes - the procedural engine is still firing but the emotional temperature drops noticeably.
